«Si les policiers ne peuvent pas nous do: “If the police can’t give us help, why are they there?” asks Marie-Mireille Bence, whose son was killed by Repentigny police last Sunday. Photo: Ridolphe Aristil
Jean René Junior Olivier avait 37 ans. I: Jean René Junior Olivier was 37. He died on August 1 after being shot three times in the chest by Repentigny police. His mother, who was worried about him, had called emergency services. The case has raised questions, worry and anger among Mr. Olivier’s loved ones and in the Repentigny community. For many, it is a tragedy that is not an isolated case and could have been avoided, since the deaths of Matthew Sheffield, Pierre Coriolan, Alain Magloire and Nicholas Gibbs, Black men with mental health problems shot by the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), could have foreshadowed it.
Pourquoi de tels événements tragiques se: Why do such tragic events happen? Crisis intervention, profiling, discrimination, stigmatization: Mr. Olivier’s loved ones and experts speak to these systemic problems, for which solutions exist.
« J’ai appelé le 911 pour venir m’aider: “I called 911 to come help me with my son,” Jean René Junior Olivier’s mother, Marie-Mireille Bence, told the media in front of her home in Repentigny the day after the tragedy. She wanted an ambulance to take Junior, as everyone called him, to the hospital. “I could see that my son had a problem. Right away I told myself that, the way he was acting, it might be a psychosis,” says Ms. Bence. She says she told the dispatcher that she wanted Mr. Olivier to get immediate help. “I told them: ‘Please, take him to a psychiatric hospital.’ I made that very clear,” she stresses.
Au moment de l’intervention, le père de: At the time of the intervention, the father of the family had a kitchen knife in his possession. “She turned to emergency services to prevent the worst, which was that her son would take his own life,” says Stanley Bazin, president of the Ligue des Noirs.
Helen Dion, directrice du Service de pol: Helen Dion, director of the Service de police de la ville de Repentigny (SPVR), said in a statement that she did not wish to comment on the intervention, since the case is in the hands of the Independent Investigations Bureau (Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes), which is responsible for shedding light on the matter. The SPVR also declined to answer our questions. The day after the tragedy, Ms. Bence spoke to the media in front of her home in Repentigny. A few days later, she addressed the crowd gathered in front of Repentigny city hall, where about a hundred people took part in a vigil in memory of the deceased. “Justice for Junior” could be read on the T-shirts, decorated with three bullet holes, that many wore for the occasion. “If I don’t speak up, I don’t know how people will interpret the way my son was shot down,” cried the grieving mother. “A police officer told me: ‘We had no choice, your son took three bullets to the stomach.’ How?” Ms. Bence said into the microphone.
Les proches de la famille et la communau: The family’s loved ones and the community are demanding answers. The victim’s mother wants to know what will happen to the officer who fired, an act that she, like many, calls criminal. “I don’t know his face, I don’t know his name,” says the victim’s son, Kayshawn Olivier, 18. “He never got the help that was requested,” says Dolmine Laguerre, Mr. Olivier’s cousin. “He seemed to be in psychosis. He had a knife, he wanted to hurt himself. His mother was in shock and didn’t know what to do. She called the police to get help. Instead of getting help, he died,” she told La Converse. Ms. Laguerre does not believe her cousin was threatening or posed a danger to others, or that he was in a position to attack the officers at the time of the intervention. She would have liked someone to invite the man to calm down. Instead, he was hit three times in the chest, something she and her loved ones cannot understand. “The police know how to aim. They could have shot somewhere else. Aiming for the heart means you want to kill him. Even his uncle, who was there, asked them to shoot him in the foot,” she says.
« Ce qui s’est passé est injuste. On rem: “What happened is unjust. Two things stand out: mental health and skin colour,” Ms. Laguerre says right off the bat. “I believe that if he had been white, this would never have happened. They would have taken him to see a psychiatrist. With him it was different, because they saw him as an animal. He’s a man, no matter what problems he had,” she adds. She also says her cousin feared the police because of the profiling and racial discrimination that run through law enforcement: “He was afraid of being shot. He wasn’t feeling well. He was sad. When you’re Black, you don’t have the right to be sad.” “White people, they don’t kill them. They protect them. My son, it’s because he’s Black [that he was killed],” notes the victim’s mother, holding back tears. Like others who spoke that evening, she cites high-profile cases of violent crimes in Quebec in which mental health played a role. The accused, who are white, are still alive.
« Alors si les policiers ne peuvent pas: “So if the police can’t give us help, why are they there?” Ms. Bence asks the gathered crowd. She only wanted her son to receive medical attention. “It’s really hard to find information about the dispatch service. We don’t really know how they operate,” says El Jones, a poet and associate professor of Political and Cultural Studies at Mount Saint Vincent University in Halifax. She believes the way mental health is described is an indicator of how emergency services are deployed in response to a call about psychological distress. “They ask whether the person is violent, or whether you’re afraid of them,” explains the poet and professor. That kind of question can lead to police being sent instead of more appropriate resources. “It’s hard to have these conversations with police services, which refuse to disclose information. We don’t even know to what extent they’re sent,” she says.
Désescalader ou désamorcer une crise, c’: De-escalating or defusing a crisis is, however, what psychosocial workers, medical staff, but also teachers and parents do regularly. “When we talk about de-escalation, we imagine something very technical, but it’s simply about talking to people with dignity and respect, and showing them that you care about them,” says Jessica Quijano, a front-line worker and spokesperson for the Defund the Police Coalition. Ms. Quijano often intervenes in crisis situations. “I’ve been doing this work for 18 years, my colleagues and I constantly intervene in situations like this one. And we don’t hurt anyone.” As she explains, it’s about reassuring the person, letting them know they’re in a safe environment, and making them understand that you’re there to help. This can be done by speaking softly, guiding them through the room, asking what’s going on or how they’re feeling, and telling them you’re there to help and that they’re safe. “It’s about making the person feel seen and taken care of. Often, the police shout, scream and act as if they were dealing with criminals,” says Ms. Quijano.
« La chose la plus difficile, c’est qu’o: “The hardest thing was that I got a call telling me people should go inside and lock the door,” says Ms. Bence, the mother of Jean René Junior Olivier. A few minutes later, her son was hit by the officers’ bullets. Ms. Quijano laments this approach, which pushes away the people who can help calm the situation. “Often the police try to isolate everyone, the people who are there or who accompany the person,” says the worker, who sometimes has to insist with authorities to be present. “The police act as if they’re afraid of the person, which is the opposite of an intervention.”
El Jones croit que les perceptions des p: El Jones believes that perceptions of people with mental health problems need to change on all sides. “We feed the idea that if you’re having a mental health crisis, you’re inherently violent, uncontrollable, which isn’t actually true,” says the professor. It would be wrong to think that because their mental health is at stake, a person is unable to express themselves. “Often, people want to talk, to be listened to. You ask them what they need, why they’re upset and what can be done for them. Then you can negotiate the situation,” she explains. “The police are trained to shoot, to manage threats, not to de-escalate.”
Cette peur se transpose également dans n: This fear also carries over into how we relate to others. We often wrongly believe that people with mental health problems are violent, which requires police help. “We immediately assume that you can’t interact with someone in crisis, go up to them and ask if they’re okay, because they might attack us,” says Ms. Jones. This feeds our tendency to call the police, a reflex that kicks in whenever a situation is perceived as dangerous, worrying or uncomfortable. To explain it, Ms. Jones cites author Robyn Maynard and her book Policing Black Lives (NoirEs sous surveillance in its French version). “We use the word ‘security’ when we talk about safety. Security is, for example, what you see in an airport,” she says. “In the popular imagination, there’s the idea that the only thing that keeps us safe is the police. This reliance on the police to resolve a situation is reinforced in our society by the media, television, culture and education.”
« Quand vous combinez la stigmatisation: “When you combine the stigmatization of mental health with anti-Black racism, individuals are portrayed as monsters and they get killed by the police,” says Ms. Jones. The numbers are telling: Black and Indigenous people are <l1>overrepresented in deaths at the hands of law enforcement</l1>, and police interventions are more likely <l2>to end in a killing when mental health is involved</l2>.
Pourquoi comptons-nous sur la police pou: Why do we count on the police for issues related to well-being and health? “It’s because we don’t have a mental health infrastructure. We use prisons, police and punishment to essentially contain and discipline people with mental health conditions,” says Ms. Jones.
Les services sociaux sont en dégringolad: Social services have been in decline for several decades following budget cuts and chronic underfunding. To fill the gap, some tasks that social services used to handle have been shifted onto law enforcement. “So there is a direct link between the elimination of all these collective services and calling on the police to fill those gaps, when their role is to tackle crime,” she explains. In her view, a complete restructuring of the mental health system is needed nationwide. The lack of support also contributes to the distress of vulnerable people, who are at greater risk of ending up in crisis.
La mort de M. Olivier ravive des souveni: Mr. Olivier’s death stirs painful memories for Yusuf Faqiri. His brother, Soleiman Faqiri, died in 2017 at the hands of law enforcement at the Lindsay jail in Ontario. He was 30. He had been locked up for 11 days without any charges against him, and died while awaiting transfer to a psychiatric institution, which had been granted three days earlier. Two investigations were carried out, but no charges were laid in this high-profile case. “It’s very moving and worrying,” Mr. Faqiri tells us, adding that he believes the situation is spreading across Canada, including Quebec. “Does that mean that the lives of people with mental health problems don’t matter?” he wonders, referring to racialized people across the country who were suffering from mental illness when they died in custody or following an intervention. He knows their names by heart. For the man who became an activist after his brother’s death, accountability is at the heart of the problem. “If you’re not held responsible for your actions, you’re going to commit these acts,” he says.
« S’il n’y a pas de responsabilité, je s: “If there’s no accountability, I’m sure there will be another tragedy soon.” Mr. Faqiri wants this accountability to show up at the legal level, but also in practices and procedures. “Why is the system so opaque? Very often, when a person dies at the hands of the police, we don’t know their name,” he notes. Efforts must be made to ensure such situations don’t happen again. To that end, he wants the police to work with communities, and not just on the surface. “They have to be equal partners. It’s not just about consultations, but about truly knowing what problems affect communities.”
Quatre ans après la mort de Soleiman Faq: Four years after Soleiman Faqiri’s death, Mr. Faqiri notes that there is more interest in mental health, a demand made all the more urgent by the pandemic. He adds sadly that, on the other hand, more and more attention is being paid to this kind of tragedy: “It’s about honouring his life, respecting him, telling his story, that’s what’s important,” he says of Jean René Junior Olivier. “What I hope is that these discussions can go far.”
Le SPVR n’a pas indiqué si les agents so: The SPVR did not say whether its officers are trained in crisis de-escalation. The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) says <l1>on its website</l1> that all its officers will be trained by 2022.
Jessica Quijano, intervenante, croit que: Jessica Quijano, a front-line worker, believes police officers can be trained, but that they shouldn’t have to intervene in psychosocial crisis situations. She is of the view that qualified, specialized first responders should be dispatched in the event of a crisis related to mental state. That is the case in Eugene, Oregon, where since 1989 Crisis Assistance Helping Out On The Streets (CAHOOTS), a mental health crisis intervention program, has been answering 911 calls.
La ville de Toronto vient de déployer un: The City of Toronto has just rolled out a pilot project with the creation of a mobile unit inspired by CAHOOTS. In New York, a pilot project will also be launched in a few neighbourhoods, aimed at preventing psychiatric crises from escalating.
La Division Urgence sociale, un projet p: The Division Urgence sociale, a pilot project set up by the Service de police de Laval (SPVL), will give social workers access to 911 calls and allow them to show up and carry out an intervention without waiting for the police. “I don’t understand why Montréal isn’t doing the same thing,” says Jessica Quijano, who wants no armed individual to be involved in these interventions.
Sur leur site web, le Service de police: On its website, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) says it responds to about a hundred mental health–related calls a year. There is a patrol made up of volunteer officers trained in crisis intervention response (RIC), whose mission is to defuse crises. The SPVM says these officers are present throughout the Montréal area, but offers no information on how they are deployed. The Équipe de soutien aux urgences psychosociales (ÉSUP), a squad of 6 police officers and 4 social workers who travel in mixed pairs, can also show up at the request of a patrol officer, but not on request during a 911 call.
